en: The Parivāra:
The Collection of Subsequent Verses, Chapter 12:
Questions and Answers on Exhortation and the Like.
For what purpose is exhortation?
For what reason is recollection?
For what purpose is the Saṅgha?
But for what purpose is the work of the mind?
It is for the purpose of admonishing and for the purpose of reminding;
the reminding is for the purpose of restraint.
The Saṅgha [performs] for the purpose of formal acceptance;
however, the preliminary deliberation (matikamma) is separate.
Do not speak in haste.
Do not speak with anger;
do not give rise to resentment,
if you are the investigator.
Do not speak hastily,
nor engage in contentious talk that is unbeneficial;
[speak] in accordance with the Sutta and the Vinaya.
In these well-established and conformable [rules],
observe the practice of inquiry as it has been performed by one who is skilled and wise.
Well-spoken and in accordance with the training rules,
not destroying one's future destiny—
strive for this, seeking your own welfare.
Speak at the proper time and what is connected to the matter.
When one has been reproved and the reprover as well,
do not hastily engage in legal dispute.
The accuser says, "He has committed an offense," while the accused says, "He has not committed one.
Without casting blame upon either, [one should investigate].
One should act according to what has been admitted; admission is established among those who are conscientious,
but it does not exist among those who are unconscientious.
Even if one who is shameless should speak much,
one should have him act according to the connection of the discourse.
What kind of person is a shameless one?
He whose promise does not take root—
this I ask you:
what kind of person is called one who lacks a sense of shame?
One intentionally commits an offense,
conceals the offense,
and goes upon a wrong path.
"Such a person is called one devoid of shame.
"Truly, I too know this:
such a person is called one devoid of shame."
And another thing I ask you:
what kind of person is called one who possesses a sense of shame?
One who does not intentionally commit an offense—
One who does not conceal an offense and does not go upon a wrong path—
such a person is called "one possessed of shame."
Truly, I too know this:
such a person is called one who possesses a sense of shame;
yet I ask you another thing.
What kind of person is called one who reproves unrighteously?
One who reproves at an improper time, with what is untrue,
harshly, and in a way that is not beneficial.
One who reproves with a mind devoid of loving-kindness, and not with a heart of mettā—
such a person is called one who reproves unrighteously.
Truly, I too know this.
Such a person is called one who reproves according to what is not Dhamma;
and now I ask you another:
what kind of person is called one who reproves according to the Dhamma?
He admonishes at the proper time, with what is true,
gentle, and beneficial;
he admonishes with a mind of loving-kindness, not with inner malice.
"Such a one is called a reprover according to the Dhamma.
Truly, I too know this:
such a one is called a reprover according to the Dhamma."
And another thing I ask you:
what kind of person is called a "foolish reprover"?
One who does not understand the sequence of what precedes and what follows.
Unskilled in what precedes and what follows,
he does not understand the sequence of the discourse;
being unskilled in the sequence of the discourse, [he fails to grasp its meaning].
Such a person is called a fool who reproaches others.
Truly, I too know this:
such a person is called a fool who reproaches others.
And I ask you another thing:
what kind of person is called a "wise reprover"?
One who understands both what precedes and what follows.
Skilled in what precedes and follows,
he knows the sequence of the discourse;
skilled in the sequence of the discourse, he understands its logical connection.
"Such a one is called a wise reprover.
"Truly, I too know this:
such a one is called a wise reprover."
And another thing I ask you:
what is called "reproving"?
One reproves for failure in virtue.
Furthermore, one reproves by way of conduct and view,
and also by way of livelihood;
thus it is called "reproof."
The collection of verses is concluded.
